item.title: L.A. Wants to Clean Up MacArthur Park. Will Fencing It Off Work?
item.description:
Los Angeles has long searched for ways to clean up MacArthur Park, to rid the space of the drug sales and homeless encampments that have made it a blight on the neighborhood and a target for the Trump administration as an example of failed Democratic leadership.

Now it is trying a new approach. The city has committed more than $2 million to erect a fence around the park that is meant to allow officials to exert more oversight over how the park is used.

Construction began on a temporary barrier on Tuesday, with a permanent fence scheduled to be completed next year. Some efforts to improve the park were already underway, including the installation of more lights around the vast 35-acre space, garbage cleanups and the deployment of more street medics and homeless service providers.

Los Angeles police and the Drug Enforcement Administration had already started to crack down on drug dealers who supply the park dwellers. In May, the agencies carried out a major raid that resulted in the arrest of 18 people who the police said were part of a network selling methamphetamine and fentanyl at the park.

Residents and merchants in the community just west of downtown Los Angeles say the recent law enforcement efforts have made a small but noticeable dent in addressing some of the problems, though they say the park remains relatively unsafe, especially at night.

The city’s plans call for the gates to be shut from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. The police will patrol the park to try to clear it out before closing.

MacArthur Park, named for the World War II general, began its life as Westlake Park in the 1880s and was once the crown jewel of the Westlake neighborhood that was home to affluent residents in the early 20th century. Over time, the park deteriorated as the wealthy fled to other areas of the city and investment in the neighborhood declined.

In the 1980s, the neighborhood became a destination for refugees and immigrants fleeing civil wars in Central America.

Today, the community is largely working class and made up of immigrants from Central America. The space features a sports field, a small auditorium, playgrounds, a recreation center and a large lake that at night reflects the downtown skyline looking east.

The park attracted national attention last summer when the Trump administration sent heavily armed Border Patrol agents and members of the National Guard to conduct a military-style sweep. The operation was intended to be a show of force, led by the ousted Border Patrol leader Gregory Bovino, and led to a confrontation between the agents and Mayor Karen Bass, who said the government was just trying to “demonstrate to the nation their bravado.”

Conservatives have also criticized local nonprofit programs that aim to reduce disease and drug deaths by providing clean syringes to users.

The fence initiative, backed by Mayor Bass and Eunisses Hernandez, the councilwoman representing the area, was undertaken by the city’s recreation and parks commission, which approved the $2.3 million project last month. A chain-link fence is being erected now to seal off a construction area for a permanent fence, which will be green and have several pedestrian entry points. The park will remain open during construction.

The plan drew praise from many in the community eager to rid the neighborhood of illicit activity, and criticism from those opposed to closing off a public space.

The president of the city’s cultural heritage organization wrote in a letter to the parks commission that a permanent fence would detract from the park’s historic character.

The cultural commission suggested instead that the city enclose the park with a more temporary barrier as it had done at Echo Park, another enclave that has struggled with many of the same issues at MacArthur Park. That barrier — a chain-link fence — was taken down after two years.

Though the fence around MacArthur Park is built to be permanent, the city plans to review its effectiveness at improving safety after three years.

On Wednesday, men in orange vests and white hard hats were erecting chain-link fencing.

Donnell Edwards, 31, one of the installers, said many of the local residents were happy to see him and his fellow workers. “They’ve been recording,” he said, adding that some had come up to thank him.

Hugo Lopez, 36, who was walking around the park with his wife and 2-year-old son on Wednesday morning, recounted getting mugged at the park one time. He said he was happy to see what he considered decisive action by the authorities.

“You can’t be here at night because people there are people who are really drugged up who can harm you,” Mr. Lopez said.

But others in the area felt the fence would be yet another eyesore, and a futile attempt at solving an intractable social problem.

“Sometimes these things make you laugh,” said Mateo Antonio, 48, as he wrapped up his morning stretch at the soccer field in the park while listening to salsa music. “This problem has nothing to do with a fence.”

People wanting to get in the park during closed hours, he said, would find a way to get in.

Deisy de Leyva, 50, was worried that homeless people who are moved out of the park would wind up outside her beauty salon across the street.

Business, she said, was already slow because of the economy, and the fear of immigration agents was already keeping many of her customers home.

Near the another section of the park, Norm Langer, 81, the owner of Langer’s Delicatessen, is perhaps the most vocal business owner on matters concerning the park. His highly popular eatery has been around since 1947 and is considered a Los Angeles institution.

“I think the fence will do wonders, but the problem still is going to exist,” Mr. Langer said, sharing Ms. de Leyva’s concern that people who need help would simply be displaced.

The hope, he said, was to see the city ensure they went somewhere to get treatment.

item.title: Spying Suspect’s Chip Network Has Ties to Chinese Military Suppliers
item.description:
Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, has extensive ties through her family and associates to China’s defense industry, according to an independent research firm and corporate filings reviewed by The New York Times.

The findings show a web of relationships, most of them indirect, linking Ms. Huang’s family and companies that acquired Nvidia chips to Chinese state-owned defense contractors that supply the People’s Liberation Army.

The nature of those relationships, including the vital question of whether Nvidia chips ended up being used to support Chinese military projects, remains murky. But the revelations, along with an investigation by The Times published on Wednesday, underscore how the Chinese effort to acquire access to the computing power of Nvidia’s chips is intertwined with Beijing’s desire to harness artificial intelligence to bolster its military capabilities.

That outcome has long been feared by U.S. national security officials, given that the technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

A confidential analysis by Strider Technologies, an independent intelligence firm that employs former intelligence officers and experts on China and specializes in corporate intelligence, shows that about $3.6 billion in Chinese government money flowed through companies associated with Ms. Huang’s family or associates. The government money funded technology projects, including data centers that received Nvidia chips.

The New York Times reviewed the Strider findings. Many of the corporate ties revealed by Strider were independently confirmed by The Times.

The Times reported last month that U.S. officials believe Ms. Huang, a Chinese citizen also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese intelligence asset who was providing information to the Ministry of State Security. The Strider Technologies analysis and the review of corporate filings by The Times show that she; her sister, Huang Yu; and an investor named Kang Wei, who was Alice Huang’s business partner and often introduced as her husband, are tied to a web of companies that connect official Nvidia partners, which can buy advanced Nvidia A.I. chips, to state- and military-linked projects.

Nvidia’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as the company’s chief executive after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang, who is no relation.

Companies in the Huang family’s network co-own a cybersecurity venture with an arm of China’s main military-electronics conglomerate, lease Nvidia-powered servers financed by an affiliate of its largest military aircraft maker and in one case share a parent company with a maker of radar and missile components.

Two companies that have partnerships with Nvidia, Megaspeed and Century Litong, are connected to Ms. Huang. Ms. Huang ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center firm that is under investigation by the Justice Department for smuggling advanced chips into China. Megaspeed has said Ms. Huang, whose involvement with Mr. Huang corresponded with a period when it was acquiring large numbers of Nvidia chips, no longer works for the company.

Ms. Huang’s family members had prominent roles and significant investments in the data center firm that founded Century Litong, which is based in Shanghai and rents out computing power to major Chinese companies and military contractors. The family members include Ms. Huang’s sister and Mr. Kang.

U.S. officials are also working to learn more about Ms. Huang and her efforts to help supply chips to data centers. The nature and extent of her ties to the P.L.A. and the companies it controls are a focus of that work, according to people briefed on the American efforts.

The ties are complex and often indirect. The research does not show whether the P.L.A. used computing power in the data centers that the family’s companies helped build. But it shows how deeply Ms. Huang and her family are intertwined with the Chinese state, and the inextricable connections between China’s tech industry and its military.

“Beijing has spent years building these networks that reach deep into Western economies,” said Greg Levesque, the chief executive of Strider. “Follow the money and, too often, you find the P.L.A. at the end of it.”

Mr. Levesque said China was exploiting more Western technology, capital and talent than ever before to build its defense industrial base. “This is happening on a scale we simply weren’t seeing a few years ago,” he said.

Nvidia declined to comment. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment. Ms. Huang could not be reached for comment.

From late last year into early this year, Century Litong appears to have been one of only a few sources able to supply Nvidia chips to China at the vast scale needed for its A.I. build-out, according to Strider.

Those chips were key to building the data centers that drive China’s A.I. development. Investigators are trying to determine how many of the chips that were used in those data centers were banned under U.S. export controls and, in essence, smuggled into the country. Companies controlled by Ms. Huang and her relatives were instrumental in supplying the chips, Strider found.

“Essentially, those entities worked around the controls to continue to meet the chip demands of the customers they already had, including at new data centers,” Mr. Levesque said.

On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the unusual step of releasing confidential information on Nvidia’s license applications to legally sell H200 chips to Chinese firms. The list showed that Nvidia had sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200s to the Hong Kong subsidiary of Century Litong.

An Nvidia spokesman said that, despite receiving some licenses, it had already stopped shipping H200s to China, and Nvidia had not and would not ship to that firm.

Century Litong has said it has no business dealings with Ms. Huang. But the company was founded in 2023 by Century Longteng, a data center operator that was then 27 percent owned by an investment firm controlled by Ms. Huang’s sister. Mr. Kang, Ms. Huang’s presumed husband, had been Century Longteng’s executive director since February 2022, according to Strider.

In 2023, Jiangsu Lettall Electronic, a Shanghai-listed maker of metal parts for flat-screen TVs, bought 90 percent of Century Litong, and owned all of it by 2024. Lettall also owns 80 percent of Nanjing Jinning Microwave, a maker of components that Lettall has said are used in Chinese radar and missile systems. Strider said Jinning’s parts go into the P.L.A.’s DF-series missiles, including intercontinental ballistic missiles and anti-ship “carrier killers,” as well as the J-20 stealth fighter plane.

China’s defense industry wants advanced A.I. chips to design better missiles and build other military software, experts have said.

Lettall did not respond to an emailed request for comment. Asked about Ms. Huang’s network of companies and their efforts to acquire chips, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said he was not familiar with the situation. “We have made clear more than once our principled position on U.S. chip exports to China,” said the spokesman, Liu Chang.

Century Litong delivered servers containing Nvidia’s H800 chips to a supercomputing center in Shanghai in October 2023, according to Strider. It is unclear where Century Litong obtained those chips, but they may have been obtained legally, since U.S. restrictions on the sale of the H800 to China did not go into effect until that same month.

Century Litong now runs servers at the Shanghai supercomputing center under a lease of about $54 million from a leasing arm of the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, China’s state aerospace and defense conglomerate.

Century Litong’s reach extends far beyond the Chinese A.I. giant Tencent. When Lettall bought into the company in 2023, it said all of Century Litong’s computing business would be housed in two places: the Tencent center in Shanghai and a data center in Shenzhen.

The Shenzhen center was built for the cloud unit of Huawei, the Chinese telecom giant that has long been under sanctions by the United States over national security concerns. Huawei awarded the project in 2022 to a company controlled by Century Longteng, according to corporate filings.

Century Litong’s customers have also included a unit of China Electronics Technology Group, or C.E.T.C., a state-owned military electronics maker. The United States has included C.E.T.C. on its list of companies that it publicly identifies as doing work with the Chinese military, banning the firm from doing work with Pentagon suppliers.

Another Century Litong partner is Hangjin Technology, a listed company whose subsidiaries make chips for China’s military.

Until last December, Hangjin controlled Chaoqing, an Nvidia partner whose website once listed High-Flyer, the hedge fund behind the Chinese A.I. start-up DeepSeek, as a partner. Others on the list included the military-linked Zhejiang Lab and its co-founder, Alibaba.

DeepSeek has attracted attention for its cutting-edge A.I. models. But lawmakers in the United States have also accused it of presenting national security risks, and the federal government has banned employees from using it. The Information earlier reported ties between Ms. Huang’s network and DeepSeek.

Hangjin did not respond to an emailed request for comment. It has said it does no business with DeepSeek.

item.title: Democrats Strengthen the Legal Line with Attorneys General Triumphs
item.description:
With The Associated Press’s late declaration on Friday that a Democrat has won the attorney general’s race in Ohio, the party wrapped up a midterm election surge that will fortify the Democrats’ legal bulwark against President Trump.

Democrats ousted two incumbents and won three additional attorney general posts that had previously been held by Republicans.

Among the incumbents defeated was Kansas’ Kris Kobach, known for writing and pushing divisive state level legislation on immigration, voting and abortion restrictions. Beyond Kansas, Democratic attorneys general have taken open posts in Iowa, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all of which are currently Republican.

Additionally, vulnerable Democratic incumbents such as Keith Ellison in Minnesota and Kris Mayes in Arizona cruised to re-election, despite Republican hopes that local concerns would overcome the national environment. Democratic newcomers easily prevailed in open contests in Michigan and Nevada as well.

With Democrats now poised to be the top law enforcement official in 29 states, they will have even more collective muscle to spearhead their party’s efforts over the last two years of the Trump administration. In the first two, Democratic attorneys general filed more than 150 cases against the administration on issues ranging from the withholding of federal funds to tariffs and the deployment of National Guard troops.

“At a time when people are worried about the rising cost of living and their rights and freedoms being put at risk, voters see that it’s Democratic A.G.s who rise to the challenge and will fight to protect them,” Sean Rankin, president of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said in a statement.

During the campaign, Republican candidates tried to sidestep questions regarding their views on state lawsuits against the Trump administration — or on Mr. Trump, whose approval ratings have sagged in Republican and Democratic states alike. Instead, they stressed local issues, such as a social services fraud scandal in Minnesota.

But Mr. Ellison won by more than 8 percentage points over Ron Schutz, a longtime trial lawyer and Republican activist. Other triumphant Democratic incumbents in battleground states included Josh Kaul in Wisconsin and Ms. Mayes in Arizona, who won by 280 votes in 2022 but more than 10 percentage points on Tuesday.

Republicans had been bullish about Michigan, where a high-profile U.S. Senate race and control of the State Legislature were also on the line. But Eli Savit, a progressive Democratic prosecutor, defeated Doug Lloyd, a Republican prosecutor, by almost 8 percentage points — the same winning margin for Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat.

In Georgia, State Representative Tanya Miller, a Democrat and former prosecutor, won by double digits. In Texas, State Senator Nathan Johnson won comfortably as well, though by a smaller winning margin than Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. Mr. Johnson will succeed Ken Paxton, the scandal-scarred attorney general of Texas who tried and failed to leap to the U.S. Senate.

“After years of A.G.s who mired the office in corruption and petty politics, today Texans said enough is enough,” Lottie Ash, political director of the Democrats’ attorney general group, said on election night.

In Kansas, Mr. Kobach, a longtime Republican lightning rod, lost to Chris Mann, a former police officer and prosecutor, by one percentage point, part of an unlikely Democratic surge in the state that saw State Senator Cindy Holscher win her race to succeed a Democratic governor and Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister in Kansas, handily beat Senator Roger Marshall.

In Iowa, Attorney General Brenna Bird lost by about two percentage points to Nate Willems, a former state representative. She outperformed Representative Ashley Hinson, who lost to State Representative Josh Turek in the U.S. Senate race, and Zach Lahn, a businessman, who was trounced by Rob Sand, the state auditor, in the governor’s race.

Republicans had better news in Florida, up and down the ticket. Attorney General James Uthmeier edged Jose Javier Rodriguez, a former state legislator, overcoming a late $5 million investment by the Democratic Attorneys General Association.

And in South Carolina, where Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat, stunned Senator Darline Graham, David Stumbo, a conservative prosecutor, won an open race to run the office which will handle the retrial of Alex Murdaugh.

Still, Adam Piper, the executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association, wrote in a memo that Tuesday’s results constituted “a category-five political hurricane” up and down the ballot.

Democrats won every statewide office in Texas and Georgia, and nearly did the same in Ohio. Moreover, Democrats scored new trifectas — controlling both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — en route to netting at least 460 legislative seats.

“With an emboldened Democrat Congress, Republican A.G.s are both America’s front line and its last line of defense when it comes to their left-wing wish list — such as court packing, the Green New Deal, Medicare for All, Second Amendment restrictions, and abolishing ICE,” Mr. Piper wrote.

item.title: Preppers Are Cashing In on Tech Anxiety
item.description:
Derrick James put in his notice at work this month.

After years working for the state of Maine, Mr. James, 52, decided the time was right to go all in on his side hustle: teaching people on the internet how to survive catastrophe. Derrick James is his online identity; he asked that his real name not be used because of concerns about revealing the location of his survival preparations in the event of a disaster.

Since 2007, he has published books on topics like defending your home, posted videos about water storage and nuclear fallout, and shared recommendations on pocketknives and camp stoves. But these days especially, there is no shortage of customers.

“I’m quitting my day job for a reason,” Mr. James said with a laugh, adding that his rates for creating a single video can start around $500. He stressed that he had been thinking about leaving for some time and added that his children getting older was another factor.

Perhaps it’s the breakdown in the nation’s aviation network, or the Microsoft outage that disrupted businesses worldwide. Or the system glitches at banks, the Apple tech failures or the malfunctioning of the National Security Agency’s internal communications. Many Americans have become nervous enough to seek the help of preppers, who are more than willing to offer counsel — and cash in while they’re at it.

There is definitely something in the water right now, Mr. James and others online say. And he can sell you a straw to filter it.

Mark Lawley, a retired law enforcement officer in North Alabama, runs a prepping Facebook group with over 100,000 members. Last year, Mr. Lawley, 69, said the group gained about 30 new members per week. This fall, that number has jumped as high as 500 people, he said.

“We don’t do bunkers. We don’t do zombies. We don’t do alien invasions,” Mr. Lawley said. “We do the things that normal people are affected by, like hurricanes and tornadoes.”

With decades of experience hunting and fishing in a culture of self-reliance in Maine, Mr. James is ready to meet the moment, but he stressed that he endorses only products he truly stands behind. He is trying to balance capitalizing on the prepping boom with not trafficking in alarmism, while protecting his identity.

Preppers are preternaturally private people, Mr. James explained. Like those who follow the rules of “Fight Club,” they can be reluctant to discuss their craft, lest they lead others to their repositories during an emergency.

Others online, however, appear to be newly dipping their toes into the prepper revenue stream.

Take a cursory scroll through TikTok and you will find plenty of users talking up battery power banks and solar lanterns. A closer inspection, however, shows many sellers have no background in emergency preparedness but do see opportunities to bump up sales.

Stacie Didomenico, 39, works in long-term care but has a TikTok account with a scant following where she regularly posts products for sale with affiliate links that give her a small cut of the profits. Usually, she’s hawking fashion and household goods.

In a typical month, Ms. Didomenico, who lives in Beacon, N.Y., said she sees a few thousand dollars in sales. Since she began peddling a portable emergency radio at the end of October, that number has jumped significantly, she said.

Victoria Still, a 39-year-old stay-at-home mother of two, saw similar success selling a combo radio-flashlight on TikTok. This week, she sold just over 200 of the tools, which she said she keeps on hand for tornadoes and other unpredictable weather in Oklahoma City. That was more than double her usual sales numbers, said Ms. Still, who has just a few thousand followers.

Liz Doncaster, a prepper content creator who lives in South Florida and focuses on practical advice for people who live alone in cities, said she was somewhat frustrated by the new influx of such creators, who she felt were “trend followers.”

A retired teacher and administrator, Ms. Doncaster, 61, said she became interested in emergency preparedness after running drills at the school where she worked. Now, she has over 100,000 followers on Instagram. She has previously been accused by some online of fear mongering, Ms. Doncaster said. In the past few weeks, that tune has changed.

She said she recently charged $10,000 for a product brand deal that required her to post nine videos over three months. During the last three weeks, her inbox has been “bombarded” by potential new business, Ms. Doncaster added.

Krystal Christensen, a content creator in Utah better known online as the Doomsday Queen, launched a webinar this week charging $15 to take a “Prepping 101” class and learn basics like how to stock an emergency pantry.

Given the increased interest in prepping, Ms. Christensen, 38, said she was committing extra time to teaching others how to ready themselves.

“We’ve set aside hours out of the day so that I can help as many people as possible,” she said.

However, she was also preoccupied with securing her own supplies, adding, “We are in overdrive prepping here.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Trump Threatens to Bar U.S. Tech Firms From Building Data Centers Abroad
item.description:
President Trump threatened on Friday to bar American technology companies from building data centers outside the United States, suggesting he could try to stymie such development by imposing a “tremendous tax” or other penalties on those businesses.

It was not clear what Mr. Trump had in mind, or how he would achieve the new prohibition. The president at one point acknowledged the tentative nature of his own announcement, which he said he had not previewed “to my people.”

Mr. Trump delivered the ultimatum at a news conference on Friday after a high-profile diplomatic trip to China. Meeting with that country’s leader, Xi Jinping, the two men discussed a vast range of economic and national security issues — including artificial intelligence, as the two superpowers race to dominate the nascent and consequential field.

The discussions coincided with fresh revelations that powerful chips made by Nvidia, a key player in the A.I. ecosystem, landed in the hands of Chinese companies, even though federal law was supposed to block such sales. That started a contested scramble inside the Trump administration to tighten its export control rules.

On Friday, Mr. Trump reiterated his support for A.I. and the sprawling data centers that help to power the technology. He praised the Claude chatbot maker Anthropic, which this week became the first frontier A.I. lab to list its shares on public markets — the largest-ever initial offering in history.

Although the speed of A.I. advancement has spooked many Americans — inciting dozens of efforts nationally to slow down data center development — Mr. Trump nonetheless doubled down in his support for those computing facilities. He promised to “fight very hard for the data centers.”

Then, Mr. Trump issued his threat to Silicon Valley.

“We’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries,” the president said, before raising the prospect that he could impose “tremendous penalties on companies that try.”

Mr. Trump described the unexplained prohibition as a way to keep ahead of China in the A.I. race.

The president’s comments came days after his administration issued a rule aimed to cut down on the ability of Chinese companies to gain access to data centers around the world. These facilities will need to obtain a license from the U.S. government before selling computing power to companies with headquarters in China.

The rule sought to close off a loophole that had allowed Chinese companies to rent A.I. compute through foreign-owned data centers, which were still allowed to buy advanced chips. The Biden administration previously explored such regulations, and Mr. Trump removed them last year — but his government later cracked down on the practice in the wake of the revelations about Nvidia.

item.title: Fact-Checking Trump’s News Conference After His Asia Trip
item.description:
President Trump repeated and revised a number of falsehoods and exaggerations during a news conference on Friday after he returned from a trip to Asia this week.

Here’s a fact-check:

What he Said

“We secured two major new trade deals. Thailand signed an agreement to eliminate all tariffs on American products — so they were charging us tremendous tariffs, it’s unbelievable, and they’re not anymore. And remove their nontariff barriers. And they want to buy $2.6 billion a year in U.S. agricultural products. … We also reached a framework trade deal with the Philippines to eliminate our trade deficit with them by slashing the Philippine tariffs on U.S. goods, we’re slashing, but dramatically increasing — so what we’re doing is, they’re going to buy 100 percent of the product from us.”

This needs context. Mr. Trump promoted two agreements that he secured during his brief visit at the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders this week. But Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said that it had agreed not to a trade deal but only to a “joint statement marking progress in negotiations.” The Philippines’ ambassador to the United States also told Reuters that nothing had been signed.

A White House fact sheet on Mr. Trump’s visit to Asia said that “once signed,” the agreement with Thailand would eliminate tariffs on 99 percent of goods imported from the United States. Thailand’s parliament also needs to pass a law to approve such a deal.

Mr. Trump said earlier in the news conference that the Philippines had agreed to buy 100 percent of agricultural imports and energy supplies from the United States — a detail not mentioned in the fact sheet. The Philippines’ Agriculture Department said this week that it was looking to secure more agricultural products from Canada and Brazil. And its president, Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., said earlier on Friday that the trade deal with the United States was still being worked out, as well as details about food and energy, according to the country’s government news agency.

What he Said

“We inherited these high prices, by the way. They talk about affordability. The affordability was caused by the Biden administration. We got the — prices are way down now.”

False. Inflation did reach a four-decade high under the Biden administration in the summer of 2022, but had fallen to 3 percent by January 2025, when Mr. Trump took office. But inflation increased after the United States attacked Iran in February.

After the war began, inflation increased to 3.3 percent in March and again to 3.8 percent in April. Inflation remained high in October, around 4 percent. Those figures are all higher than inflation at the end of the Biden administration.

Other Claims

The president repeated a number of other claims The New York Times has previously fact-checked:

He asserted that more Americans are working today than ever before. (This is a meaningless statistic, given population growth. The unemployment rate in October was a low 4.1 percent, compared with 4 percent in January 2025, when he took office.)

He overstated credit for settling eight wars. (It is an exaggeration to call some of the conflicts “wars,” and some countries dispute Mr. Trump’s role in others.)

He overstated the trade deficit with Canada as $80 billion. (It was about $27 billion last year.)

He claimed, with no evidence, that “fentanyl coming into our country by boat, by ship, by water, sea, oceans is down 97 percent.” (As evidence of this figure, the White House previously cited a five-month dip in marijuana seized by one branch of one federal agency.)
